title: Offline Preference-Based Trajectory Evaluation
claim: Binary success metrics tie trajectories that differ in partial progress or timing, hiding distinctions that trajectory-aware comparison could reveal.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right, formulas as captions under each plot
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the same axes: time on the x-axis and return on the y-axis. A light gray horizontal line near the top is labeled 'success'. Each plot shows two step-function return curves, a red one labeled f and a green one labeled f′. In panel (a), both curves stay below the success line. The red curve rises higher than the green one, so the trajectories differ in partial progress, yet both end in failure. The caption reads μ_SR(f) = μ_SR(f′) = 0. In panel (b), both curves reach the success line, red earlier than green. The caption reads μ_SR(f) = μ_SR(f′) = 1. The red and green contrast draws the eye first, and the equal success-rate equations underneath make the point that the metric ties.
caption: Trajectory ties under success rate. \subref{fig:tied-failures} Two unsuccessful trajectories can be distinguished by partial terminal returns. \subref{fig:tied-successes} Two successful trajectories can be distinguished by accumulation of return over time.
abstract: Offline evaluation of agentic systems often collapses trajectories into a binary terminal success value, discarding information about partial progress. This, in turn, results in widespread ties that create statistical inefficiency by reducing effective sample size and weakening the ability to distinguish systems. We propose preference-based trajectory evaluation, an evaluation measure that compares pairs of trajectories directly by using temporal preferences between time-to-return profiles. We find that, across diverse agentic and interactive benchmarks, success-based metrics result in tied comparisons on roughly 75% of instances, while trajectory-aware preferences reduce ties to roughly 35%, improving discriminative power, ranking stability, and data efficiency. Our results suggest that benchmark saturation, often portrayed as the result of poor data collection or problem difficulty, may also be explained by the design of the evaluation measure.
